title: Lietuvoje kriketą žaidžiantys indai: mūsų tikslas – atnešti šį žaidimą į šalį
content:
Savaitgaliais Vilniaus Vingio parke sportuojantys ir vaikštantys žmonės jau galėjo nustebti pamatę netikėtą treniruotę prie estrados esančioje pievoje. Kelis kartus per mėnesį čia renkasi Lietuvoje gyvenantys Pietų Azijos piliečiai ir žaidžia tai, ką gimtinėje žaidė nuo mažumės, – kriketą.
Kriketas dažnai minimas tarp populiariausių pasaulio sporto šakų. Dėl strategijos gausos kriketas kartais lyginamas su beisbolo ir šachmatų deriniu, sutraukiantis milijardus sirgalių Indijoje, Pakistane, Bangladeše ar Šri Lankoje.
2025 m. Tarptautinės kriketo tarybos „Champions Trophy“ finalas tarp Indijos ir Naujosios Zelandijos tapo vienu žiūrimiausių kriketo mačų istorijoje. Vien Indijoje transliaciją stebėjo apie 230 mln. žiūrovų, finalo metu buvo pasiekti rekordiniai televizijos ir skaitmeninių platformų auditorijos rodikliai.
Kriketo istorija ir taisyklės
Kriketo istorija skaičiuoja daugiau kaip keturis šimtus metų. Žaidimas atsirado Anglijoje, o Britų imperijos laikais išplito po visą pasaulį. Šiandien kai kuriose šalyse jis daugiau nei sportas – nacionalinės tapatybės dalis. Kriketo žaidimų trukmė – skirtinga.
Tradicinis aukščiausio lygio kriketo formatas gali trukti iki penkių dienų, tačiau vėliau atsirado vienos dienos ir trumpesni T20 formatai, trunkantys apie 3 valandas.
Nors pirmą kartą stebint rungtynes taisyklės gali pasirodyti painios, pagrindinis tikslas gana paprastas. Viena komanda muša kamuoliuką ir renka taškus bėgdama tarp vartelių, o kita stengiasi mušėjus sustabdyti. Būtent strategijos ir taktikos gausa dažnai minima kaip viena iš priežasčių, kodėl kriketas laikomas itin sudėtingu komandiniu sportu.
Šeima virtusi kriketo bendruomenė
Iš Indijos į Lietuvą prieš ketverius metus dirbti atvykęs Taufeeqas Shaikas sako, kad kriketas jam pažįstamas nuo mažumės, jį žaidžia visų amžių žmonės. O atvykęs į Lietuvą ieškojo to, kas pažįstama.
„O kai atvykau į Vilnių ir atradau „Facebooke“ grupę žmonių, kurie čia žaidžia kriketą, nusprendžiau prie jų prisijungti. Po to supratau, kad žmonės rimtai žaidžia šį žaidimą. Taip padidėjo ir mano susidomėjimas – ne tik žaisti kriketą, bet ir auginti bendruomenę, atnešti šį žaidimą į Lietuvą“, – sakė T. Shaikas.
Atviroje vietoje žaidžiamas žaidimas sulaukia ir daugelio smalsių žvilgsnių. Lietuvio akiai šis žaidimas gana neįprastas. Kriketo žaidėjai pasakoja, kad aikštelėje dažnai tenka ne tik žaisti, bet ir aiškinti taisykles smalsiems praeiviams. Kai kurie vėliau grįžta išbandyti šio sporto patys.
„Jie klausia, koks čia žaidimas. Daug žmonių nežino. Bet kas žino, ateina ir klausia. [...] Lietuviai klausia, bando suprasti šį žaidimą, o mes – paaiškinti. Taip pat bandome juos kviesti pasitreniruoti, išbandyti šį žaidimą“, – pasakojo T. Shaikas.
Konkurencija už aikštelės ribų dingsta
Kriketo bendruomenė Lietuvoje kol kas nėra didelė, tačiau aktyvi. Šiuo metu šalyje veikia keturi klubai: Vilniaus kriketo klubas, „Aquila“ kriketo klubas, Kauno kriketo klubas ir „Falcon“ kriketo klubas. Aktyviai žaidžiančiųjų bendruomenę sudaro apie 60 žmonių. Dauguma jų – Lietuvoje dirbantys ar studijuojantys užsieniečiai iš Pietų Azijos šalių.
Žaidėjai pasakoja, kad sportinio azarto žaidžiant netrūksta ir klubų akistatos primena lietuviams itin pažįstamą Vilniaus „Ryto“ ir Kauno „Žalgirio“ krepšinio klubų susitikimą.
Nors maždaug 60–65 metrų apskritime, kuriame ir žaidžiamas kriketas, įtampos tarp komandų yra, žaidimui pasibaigus jie vėl tampa artimais draugais, besidžiaugiantys už kitų pergales.
„Aš iš vieno Indijos regiono, kiti mano komandos žaidėjai – iš kitų Indijos regionų. Kai susirenkame žaisti kartu, tampame lyg šeima. Dauguma žmonių, su kuriais kartu žaidžiame kriketą Lietuvoje, yra artimi mano draugai“, – teigė T. Shaikas.
Didžiausias sunkumas
Augančiai bendruomenei tenka susidurti ir su problemomis. Didžiausia jų – tinkamos aikštelės trūkumas. Profesionaliam kriketui reikalingas specialiai paruoštas paviršius, o tokių vietų Lietuvoje praktiškai nėra. Pasiruošti treniruotei užtrunka bene valandą – audinys, kuris tampa aikštele, įtempiamas ir įkalamas į žemę.
Net ir stebint žaidimą girdisi, kada kamuoliukas atšoka netinkamai būtent dėl aikštelės nelygumų. Todėl oficialios kriketo varžybos dažniausiai vyksta ne Lietuvoje, o kaimyninėje Latvijoje ir Estijoje, kur jau yra profesionalių kriketo aikštelių.
„Pirminis iššūkis yra žaidimo aikštelė. Manau, ir patys matėte, kaip ilgai trunka ir kaip sunku paruošti žaidimui tinkamą aikštelę. Mes ieškome pagalbos, kad padėtų paruošti aikštelę tinkamai, tęsiame pokalbius su ministerija, padedame jiems suprasti. Nes šiuo metu kriketas nėra toks populiarus žaidimas.
Taigi dabar esame patenkinti tuo, ką turime. Bet jei norime, kad žaidėjų gretos augtų, vyktų varžybos su klubais iš kitų šalių, ši aikštelė nėra tam tinkama“, – pabrėžė T. Shaikas.
Domisi mokyklos
Vis dėlto entuziastai sako matantys teigiamų ženklų. Mokyklos vis dažniau domisi galimybe supažindinti mokinius su šiuo sportu, o Lietuvoje dirba ir keli Tarptautinės kriketo tarybos sertifikuoti treneriai.
Vienas jų – Vinayagasundaramas Subramanis, save kviečiantis vadinti Vinay, supranta, koks neįprastas ir ilgas jo vardas lietuviams.
„Kriketo žaidimas Lietuvoje man suteikė tiek daug. Gavau Tarptautinės kriketo tarybos sertifikatą ir galiu keliauti į mokyklas mokyti vaikų. Kriketas suteikė ir draugysčių, kurių kitaip neturėčiau. Jie praeina pro šalį ir klausia, ką mes čia žaidžiame. Kai pasakome, kad varžybose žaidžiame už Lietuvą, jie tuo labai didžiuojasi.
Niekada nesu matęs nė vieno, kuris ateitų ir piktai ant mūsų šauktų, kad užimame jo vietą. Tai Lietuvoje tiesiog nevyksta. Lietuviai labai šiltai priima, jie geraširdžiai. Mes jaučiamės dalimi“, – tvirtino jis.
Ramina lietuviška tyla
V. Subramanis, paklaustas, kas labiausiai patinka gyvenant Lietuvoje, teigia, kad tyla.
„Man labai patinka, kad Lietuva tokia tyli. Indijoje viskas vyksta daug greičiau, o čia žmonės tokie geri. Aš čia jau aštuonerius metus, tiek daug žmonių čia kalba apie mane gražiai, išmokau kalbą, kol dirbau prekybos centre. Žmonės čia labai geri, jie išmoksta daugiau apie mano kultūrą, o aš – apie jų“, – tvirtino pašnekovas.
Nors susidraugavę kriketo komandų nariai palaiko vienas kitą, labiausiai žaisdamas kriketą jis pasigenda tikrosios šeimos palaikymo.
„Pasiilgsti tik vieno – tave už aikštelės ribų palaikančių draugų ir šeimos. Tai vienintelis dalykas, kurio trūksta. Bet čia turime palaikančius komandos narius. Kartais net transliuojame varžybas, kai žaisti keliaujame į kitas Europos šalis“, – pasakoja V. Subramanis.

title: Emotion-regulation training reduces distress, changes the brain, team reports
content:
CHAMPAIGN, Ill. — A five-week training intervention taught college students to better regulate their emotions in response to negative events, a new study finds. After the training, the students reported less emotional distress when viewing negative images or thinking about difficult events from their own lives, and brain scans revealed corresponding changes in the spontaneous functional connectivity of their brains.
The findings are detailed in the journal Scientific Reports.
The new work builds on insights from a 2021 study of emotional resilience in veterans. That study trained the veterans to use two emotion-regulation strategies: one in which they focused their attention on neutral contextual features of photos or memories of negative events, and the other a method called “cognitive reappraisal,” which involved reflecting on the potentially positive dimensions of otherwise distressing memories or images. The veterans who were trained in these techniques experienced less emotional distress in response to the memories and images afterward, the researchers found. Functional MRI brain scans also showed changes in how the trainees processed cognitive and emotional information.
“After seeing promising results in veterans, we extended the intervention to college students,” said University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign psychology professor Sanda Dolcos, who led the new work with Kelly Hohl, a postdoctoral resident at the Phoenix VA Healthcare Center, and U. of I. psychology professor Florin Dolcos. “We wanted to know whether training in the flexible use of focused attention and cognitive reappraisal could help young adults develop more adaptive responses to stress, while also uncovering the cognitive mechanisms supporting resilience.”
The researchers wanted to test the same emotion-regulation techniques in young people experiencing low-level chronic stress at a time in their lives when brain systems supporting self-regulation continue to mature. While veterans face significant stress, including trauma-related symptoms, college students encounter different but important challenges related to academic demands, social transitions and emerging adulthood, Sanda Dolcos said.
For the focused-attention training, “we taught the college students to focus on the background of certain emotional images,” she said. “We directed them to look more at the neutral, more contextual aspects of a scene.”
In a photo of a traffic accident, for example, participants might practice focusing on background elements such as trees, intact cars on the roadway or a blue sky.
“Eye-tracking research has shown that emotion regulation is reflected in modulations of gaze patterns,” the researchers wrote. Reducing one’s fixation on the emotional parts of an image and turning one’s attention to neutral background elements has been found to aid in regulating emotions.
For the cognitive reappraisal training, researchers asked participants to practice reinterpreting potentially negative emotional situations in a more positive light. These situations included those depicted in photos provided by the researchers as well as the students’ own experiences.
The participants engaged in the training exercises twice a week for five weeks. The researchers also encouraged them to practice the emotion-regulation techniques in their daily lives.
Before and after the training, the students answered questions about their mood, levels of anxiety and worry and potential PTSD symptoms. Most of those in the training group also underwent neuroimaging scans while awake but not engaged in a task. This approach captures a person’s spontaneous, or resting state “functional connectivity,” a baseline measure of how various brain regions communicate with one another.
Follow-up questionnaires, eye-tracking patterns and brain scans revealed that participants were increasingly engaged in the focused attention method and relied less on cognitive reappraisal. The trainees experienced less emotional distress in response to negative images and memories at the end of the five weeks than at the beginning, and less than those in the control group, who were not trained. They spent less time looking at emotionally charged areas of pictures without being prompted to do so.
The brain scans revealed significant changes in the way different brain networks were communicating, with more reliance on “top-down” versus “bottom-up” processing after the training, the researchers said.
Top-down processing involves several brain structures, many in the prefrontal cortex at the front of the brain behind the forehead, while bottom-up processing engages the limbic system, including brain regions like the amygdala, which lie deeper within the brain, the researchers said.
“Bottom-up processing helps us detect and respond to important information in our environment; whereas top-down processing allows us to intentionally guide our attention and responses based on our goals,” Hohl said. “For adaptive functioning, the brain needs to flexibly balance both processes.”
The brain scans of trained individuals revealed more connectivity in parts of the prefrontal cortex, and “a reduction in the sensitivity of regions associated with negative emotions” after the training, Florin Dolcos said. The training also led to more efficient brain connectivity, he said.
The study shows that emotional resilience is something that can be trained, and the evidence for that is seen in the documented changes in behavior and in the brain, Sanda Dolcos said.
“We are seeing that resilience is about flexibility,” she said. “The key to resilience is not avoiding negative emotions or just simply trying to feel positive all the time; it’s more about developing the flexibility to respond to emotions in ways that fit the situation.”
A follow-up analysis is more closely examining the impact of training on the participants’ written narratives of their distressing memories and the associated brain changes, the researchers said.
Sanda and Florin Dolcos are faculty in the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology at the U. of I.

title: Cachorro desaparecido brinca aos pés de repórter ao vivo e reencontra tutora mais de 1 mês depois; vídeo
content:
Cachorro desaparecido brinca aos pés de repórter ao vivo e reencontra tutora mais de 1 mês depois; vídeo
Um cachorro desaparecido reencontra tutora em Salvador, BA, depois de uma participação inesperada na televisão. Negão apareceu brincando aos pés do repórter Lisboa Júnior durante uma transmissão ao vivo da TV Bahia, na última quarta-feira (26), e o vídeo acabou chegando justamente à família que o procurava havia mais de um mês.
Negão estava desaparecido desde 5 de julho e era procurado pela tutora havia mais de um mês. Depois que o vídeo começou a circular nas redes, as imagens chegaram até ela, que reconheceu o companheiro imediatamente e conseguiu descobrir onde ele estava.
“Pense em um dog carinhoso e brincalhão!”, escreveu Lisboa ao compartilhar a cena. O jornalista explicou que não conseguiu retribuir a brincadeira durante o vivo porque, naquele momento, apresentava uma notícia sobre uma morte.
Brincadeira começou antes da transmissão
Lisboa estava em frente ao Hospital Geral do Estado, no bairro de Brotas, quando Negão se aproximou pouco antes de o repórter entrar no ar no BATV.
Os dois chegaram a brincar enquanto as câmeras ainda não estavam transmitindo. Depois, o cachorro se afastou e parecia ter seguido o próprio caminho.
Quando o jornal começou, porém, ele apareceu novamente com um pedaço de tecido na boca e se acomodou junto ao jornalista. Foi essa segunda aproximação que acabou registrada ao vivo e ganhou as redes sociais.
Leia mais notícia boa sobre pets
- Filme sobre Shurastey e Jesse Koz ganha data de estreia nos cinemas: nas férias
- Dia Mundial do Cachorro: 7 histórias emocionantes de cães heróis que salvaram vidas
- Cachorrinha entra na água debaixo de casa para resgatar filhote; todos foram salvos; vídeo
Família procurava Negão desde julho
Negão havia sumido do bairro de São Caetano, também em Salvador, no dia 5 de julho. Segundo Gleicielle, irmã da tutora, o desaparecimento aconteceu no dia do último jogo do Brasil na Copa e deu início a uma busca que durou semanas.
“Desde então começamos uma procura incansável e, de repente, ela vê na sua reportagem. Foi Deus mostrando depois de muitas orações”, contou Gleicielle ao comentar a publicação de Lisboa.
A irmã disse ainda que a tutora reconheceu Negão assim que viu o vídeo no Instagram do jornalista. A aparição na televisão finalmente deu à família uma pista concreta de onde procurar.
Morador em situação de rua acolheu o cachorro
Durante o período longe de casa, Negão também recebeu ajuda.
Segundo Gleicielle, um morador em situação de rua havia acolhido o animal. Lisboa chegou a vê-los próximos e, inicialmente, acreditou que o cachorro pudesse pertencer ao homem.
Quando a família chegou à região depois de reconhecer Negão na reportagem, o próprio morador entregou o cão à irmã da tutora para que ele pudesse voltar para casa.
O encontro aconteceu em Brotas, a aproximadamente 12 quilômetros de São Caetano. Ainda não se sabe por onde Negão passou até chegar tão longe do bairro onde vivia.
Vídeo virou a pista que faltava
Mais de um mês de buscas terminou depois de uma participação na TV que ninguém havia planejado.
O cachorro desaparecido apareceu diante das câmeras apenas tentando conseguir alguns minutos de atenção, mas a repercussão das imagens fez com que alguém da própria família o reconhecesse.
Para Gleicielle, o desfecho veio depois de muitas orações e tentativas de encontrá-lo. Para o homem que o acolheu nesse intervalo, significou também entregar o novo companheiro de volta a quem vinha procurando por ele.
Lisboa comemorou o final feliz
O repórter soube depois que o cachorro que havia conhecido durante o trabalho já estava novamente com a família.
“Poder ajudar uma tutora a reencontrar o seu companheiro e devolver um pouco de tranquilidade para os dois é uma alegria que não tem preço”, afirmou Lisboa ao g1.
A afinidade com Negão também não veio do nada. Lisboa é tutor de Zeca, um american bully de 5 anos que é doador de sangue. O jornalista tem até o rosto e o nome do cachorro tatuados na perna esquerda.
No fim, aquela entrada ao vivo ganhou um desfecho que ninguém na equipe poderia prever: além de render uma cena fofa para quem assistia ao jornal, mostrou à família exatamente onde Negão estava.

title: Ticketverkäufe: Kinos erleben bestes Halbjahr seit Corona
content:
Ticketverkäufe : Kinos erleben bestes Halbjahr seit Corona
Im ersten Halbjahr 2026 sind deutlich mehr Menschen ins Kino gegangen als in den Jahren zuvor. Es könnte das stärkste Kinojahr seit Beginn der Pandemie werden. An welchen Filmen liegt das?
Das Kinojahr 2026 könnte sich nach Einschätzung der Filmförderungsanstalt (FFA) zum stärksten seit der Pandemie entwickeln. Im ersten Halbjahr wurden rund 47,5 Millionen Eintrittskarten verkauft und rund 502,2 Millionen Euro Umsatz gemacht, wie die FFA in Berlin mitteilte. Das waren fast sieben Millionen Kinokarten mehr als im Vorjahreszeitraum (+16,9 Prozent). Der Umsatz stieg um fast 100 Millionen Euro (+24,5 Prozent).
Die erste Jahreshälfte habe den Kinos das beste Ergebnis seit der Corona-Pandemie beschert, so die FFA. Im Vergleich zur ersten Jahreshälfte 2019 wurden zwar immer noch rund sechs Millionen Eintrittskarten weniger verkauft. Der Umsatz sei aber leicht um neun Prozent gestiegen. Dies dürfte auch mit gestiegenen Eintrittspreisen zusammenhängen. Die Branche schaue mit großer Zuversicht auf die kommenden Monate, sagte FFA-Vorstand Peter Dinges.
Nach Einschätzung der FFA könnten bis zum Jahresende insgesamt rund 100 Millionen Tickets verkauft werden, insbesondere die Kinostarts von „Spider-Man: Brand New Day“ und Christopher Nolans „Die Odyssee“ lockten viele Menschen ins Kino. In englischsprachigen Medien kursieren für den Erfolg der Blockbuster Wortschöpfungen wie „Spodyssey“. Zum Vergleich: 2019 waren rund 119 Millionen Karten an Kinokassen gelöst worden.
Die meisten Menschen gingen im ersten Halbjahr 2026 ins Kino, um den Animationsfilm „Der Super Mario Galaxy Film“ zu sehen – rund 3,7 Millionen Tickets wurden verkauft. Dahinter folgt das Michael Jackson-Biopic „Michael“ mit etwa 2,8 Millionen gelösten Karten. Auf dem dritten Platz landet die Fortsetzung des Films „Der Teufel trägt Prada 2“ (rund 2,6 Millionen Tickets). Hinter der Fortsetzung „Avatar: Fire and Ash“ (rund 2,5 Millionen Tickets) schafft es mit „Extrawurst“ ein deutscher Film unter die besten fünf Filme. Fast zwei Millionen Menschen sahen die Komödie mit Hape Kerkeling.

title: A Tamil Nadu Teacher Turned His Govt School’s Classrooms Into Bright Train Coaches & Enrolment Tripled
content: After months of attending classes online during the COVID pandemic, Manimekalai remembers finally walking back into Pethanayakanur Government High School in Coimbatore district. The school she returned to looked very different. Every classroom had been painted to resemble a colourful train coach. Music and celebrations welcomed the students back after months away from their teachers and friends. “During the COVID pandemic, we had online classes. When we finally returned to school, we were amazed to see all the classrooms painted like train coaches. Sir welcomed us with music and celebration. It was unforgettable,” recalls Manimekalai, now a Class 10 student. The idea had come from Balamurugan, the school’s Tamil teacher, who wanted children returning after the pandemic to feel excited about coming back to school. After COVID, the school painted its classrooms to resemble train coaches for returning students. For Manimekalai, the train coaches are part of a school she speaks about with pride. For Balamurugan and his colleagues, they represent one colourful chapter in a transformation that had begun almost a decade earlier. Long before the classrooms looked like train coaches, Pethanayakanur Government High School was struggling to convince parents to send their children there. Before the train coaches, there were only 70 students In 2012, the school had around 70 students. Its infrastructure and facilities were relatively poor, affecting how parents perceived the school. Families also had other options nearby. A larger government higher secondary school around 2 km away had more than 400 students, while another higher secondary school about 5 km away had over 900. Many parents chose these better-established schools or private schools for their children. Then, in 2013, Balamurugan joined Pethanayakanur Government High School as a Tamil teacher. The change that followed came in stages. He became the primary driving force during its initial years, beginning with the physical environment around the children. As the initiatives grew, other teachers joined him, and the work gradually became a collective effort by the teaching staff. Pethanayakanur Government High School now has more than 210 students, up from 70 in 2012. Between 2013 and 2015, one of Balamurugan’s first priorities was the barren school grounds. “In one week, we planted 110 saplings. Today, those trees give shade to our children,” he says. What began with those first saplings would eventually grow into a wider effort to make environmental learning part of school life. The first changes took root in the school grounds From 2015 to 2017, environmental activities expanded. Students began collecting native seeds, making seed balls and participating in programmes around biodiversity and environmental conservation. Over the years, they have made 45,000 seed balls for reforestation drives and planted more than 960 saplings across the campus and neighbourhood. They have also attended seminars on forests, biodiversity and climate change. “Climate change will shape their lives. We want our students to grow up respecting nature,” says Balamurugan. Students have planted more than 960 saplings across the campus and neighbourhood over time. That thinking appears in small practices across the campus too. The school works towards maintaining a green, clean and plastic-free environment. During birthday celebrations, for instance, students are encouraged to avoid plastic-packaged chocolates and share jaggery or homemade sweets instead. For Balamurugan, environmental education works best when children can participate in it themselves, whether by planting a sapling, collecting a native seed or writing about the world around them. That last activity, writing, would soon become another important part of the school’s transformation. A library grew, and students began seeing themselves as writers Between 2017 and 2019, the school increased its focus on reading and student participation. A small library that had been developed earlier began to grow. Reading programmes and student reading circles followed, encouraging children to pick up books, discuss what they had read and eventually write their own poems, essays and stories. Today, the library holds more than 6,000 books. It was built book by book through several sources. The school library now holds more than 6,000 books built through donations and teacher support. Balamurugan, who participates in reading circles in Pollachi and Coimbatore and has written books himself, reached out to reading groups, writers, readers and non-profit organisations for donations. He also bought books personally, spending around Rs 24,000 on them. Government departments contributed books as well. Inside that library, Class 9 student Tamil Arasi has begun to see herself differently. “In most places, students read the works of famous authors. But in our school, students read our own poems and articles in books,” she says with a soft laugh. “It makes us feel like real writers.” Students’ short stories, essays and poems have also been published in book form with support from Balamurugan. “The short stories, essays and poems we write have been published as a book by some of the publishers, with the help of Teacher Balamurugan. Our books are read by other readers as well,” Tamil Arasi says. Her own writing has travelled far beyond her classroom. “He had sent my article on environmental protection for the Tamil Nadu Government's student magazine, Thenchittu. My article has been published in this journal. More than 8 lakh students have read this article. We are running a readers’ circle under the leadership of a Tamil teacher,” she says happily. Tamil Arasi’s environmental article was published in the Tamil Nadu student journal Thenchittu. For Tamil Arasi, seeing her work in print has made writing feel tangible. Children at the school can now pick up books and encounter words written by classmates sitting beside them. As this reading culture grew, the school was also finding other ways for children to connect with their roots and discover what they enjoyed beyond textbooks. From books to folk arts, learning began spilling beyond the classroom By 2019 and 2020, Pethanayakanur Government High School had developed a broader learning environment combining academics with environmental activities, reading, Tamil folk arts and sports. Students trained in traditional forms such as Parai Isai (parai drumming), Mayilattam (peacock dance), Oyilattam (folk dance), Karakattam (pot-balancing folk dance), Kavadiyattam (kavadi dance) and Kummi (clapping folk dance). Manimekalai says the school day stretches from morning into the evening. After regular classes, students receive two hours of training in traditional Tamil folk arts. They also take part in tree planting and sports sessions. For her, these experiences are part of what makes the school special. “My brother studied here and has now cleared NEET, India's toughest medical entrance exam,” she says. “I’m proud to study in this school. Our Tamil teacher, Balamurugan Sir, treats us like his own children.” Students receive two hours of training in Tamil folk arts such as Parai Isai after classes. Her brother studied at Pethanayakanur Government High School until Class 10, completed Class 12 at another government school, and later cleared NEET. “That’s a big win for our school. I feel lucky and proud to study here,” she adds. By the time the pandemic arrived, many of the pieces were already in place: trees that students had helped plant, reading circles, a growing library, environmental activities, cultural programmes and sports. The long closure then created a new question for the teachers: How could they make children feel happy about returning? Rs 50,000 turned ordinary classrooms into colourful train coaches The answer became the feature that visitors now notice as soon as they enter the school. Following the COVID period, the classrooms were painted to resemble bright train coaches, creating a colourful and welcoming environment for returning students. The makeover cost around Rs 50,000. Balamurugan contributed Rs 35,000 himself, while parents contributed the remaining Rs 15,000. Balamurugan contributed Rs 35,000 towards the Rs 50,000 train-themed classroom makeover. The train-themed classrooms were one part of a larger combination of personal contributions, parent support, donations and government assistance that helped the school develop over the years. The Tamil Nadu School Education Department provided the smart classroom and also contributed books to the library. Other resources came through Balamurugan’s networks of readers, writers and non-profit organisations, while teachers and parents became part of the school’s growing efforts. For the students returning after the pandemic, however, those funding streams translated into something far simpler: classrooms that made school feel exciting again. Manimekalai still remembers that first day back. The transformation also appears in another number that the teachers and headmistress point to with pride: enrolment. Class 10 student Manimekalai remembers returning after COVID to the train-themed classrooms. Parents began choosing the school again From around 70 students in 2012, Pethanayakanur Government High School now has more than 200. Headmistress Umamaheswari puts the current figure at more than 210. “In 2012, we had only 70 students. Today we have more than 210. Parents send their children here because they see how disciplined, confident, and responsible they become,” she says. The rise happened gradually as parents saw changes in the school environment, facilities, academic performance and the opportunities available to students. The school has maintained a 100% Class 10 pass rate from 2015, according to the information shared by the school. Students have also participated in and recorded achievements across sports, art and craft and other activities. The school has maintained a 100% Class 10 pass rate since 2015, according to school records. For Umamaheswari, the commitment of the teaching staff has shaped much of that progress. “If every school had teachers as constructive and committed as ours, our children’s future would be even brighter,” she says. The numbers tell one part of the story. The children reveal another. A student sees her environmental article appear in a government magazine. Another speaks proudly about a brother who once studied in the same classrooms and went on to clear NEET. Children learn folk dances after lessons, collect seeds, make seed balls and sit beneath trees planted years earlier. For Balamurugan, all of these activities lead towards the same purpose. ‘We want them to become good thinkers and good human beings’ For Balamurugan, the transformation of Pethanayakanur Government High School has always centred on the children who walk through its gates. “Whether it is reading, writing, folk arts, or environmental education, everything we do is to help students become good thinkers and good human beings,” he says. Balamurugan joined the school in 2013 and helped lead its transformation over the following years. Thirteen years after he joined the school, some of the earliest saplings planted on its grounds now provide shade to its students. Inside, a library that began small holds more than 6,000 books. Student writing sits alongside the work they read. Traditional Tamil arts continue after classroom lessons. The walls themselves resemble train coaches, created to welcome children back to a place their teachers wanted them to enjoy. And where around 70 students studied in 2012, more than 200 do today. For children like Tamil Arasi and Manimekalai, the transformation is part of their everyday school life: the stories they write, the arts they learn, the trees they care for, and the confidence with which they talk about where they study. “I feel lucky and proud to study here,” says Manimekalai.

title: Refugee passes GCSEs after fleeing war-torn Sudan
content:
Refugee passes GCSE after fleeing war-torn Sudan
- Published
A refugee who fled a war-torn country and found safety in the UK before becoming a football referee says he has proved "you can achieve your goals" after passing his GCSEs.
Nasser Hamid grew-up in a "tiny" village in Sudan, where millions have been displaced since the country's civil war began in 2023.
The 20-year-old, who was 16 at the time and could not speak English, fled his home and moved to Ipswich, where he was helped by Suffolk Refugee Support.
After passing GCSE English earlier this year, he has now achieved grade 4 in maths and said it was "one of the proudest moments in my life".
When Hamid arrived in the UK, he stayed in accommodation provided by YMCA Suffolk along with other people who only spoke Arabic.
He requested to be moved to a different shared housing block, with people who could help him learn English, and he also worked at Portman Road as a cashier.
More stories from Suffolk:
Hamid, whose mother and younger brothers remain in Sudan, said it was important to "just believe in yourself".
"With discipline and hard work, you can achieve your goals," he added.
"Thanks to Suffolk New College, without their help I wouldn't be standing here."
An injury ended his dreams of becoming a footballer and he has qualified as a referee with the help of the Ipswich Town Foundation.
He has overseen a charity game at Portman Road and officiated Saturday and Sunday league matches.
"I went to the Edinburgh International Cup and I'd like to continue to progress – to the Championship, the Premier League, and the World Cup, who knows," he said.
Hamid now wants to become an engineer.
David Squire, head of maths at Suffolk New College and Hamid's teacher, said: "I've never been prouder of a learner in my life."

title: Regata Cei Newydd yn 'gyfle i ddathlu ein treftadaeth'
content:
Regata Cei Newydd yn 'gyfle i ddathlu ein treftadaeth'
- Cyhoeddwyd
Mae regata Cei Newydd wedi bod yn rhan o fywyd y dre ers y 19eg ganrif ac yn dathlu carreg filltir arbennig eleni gan ei bod yn cael ei chynnal am y 150fed tro.
Mae'r regata'n cael ei chynnal rhwng 18-20 o Awst a bu Huw Williams, sy'n aelod o Fwrdd Goruchwylio Cei Newydd ac yn un o'r rhai sy'n trefnu'r digwyddiad ym Mae Ceredigion, yn siarad ar Dros Frecwast ar Radio Cymru.
Dywedodd: "Mae lot yn mynd 'mlaen yng Nghei Newydd dros y tri diwrnod. Bydd cychod yn hwylio, bydd 'na nofio, rhwyfo, a phob math o hwyl a sbri i'r teulu gyfan.
Uchafbwynt
"Mae'n ddigwyddiad mawr yng Nghei Newydd. Mae mis Awst wastad yn fishi yma ond mae wythnos y regata bron pob blwyddyn yr wythnos fwyaf prysur ni'n cael fan hyn.
"Mae cychod hwylio yn dod ar draws Bae Ceredigion ac mae pobl yn dod i ymweld ac i gymryd rhan yn y nofio a'r rhwyfo a phob math o gystadlaethau sydd 'da ni."
Gyda'r dref yn fwrlwm yn ystod y regata, mae Huw yn pwysleisio pwysigrwydd yr ŵyl fel dathliad o dreftadaeth Cei Newydd: "Dechreuodd y regata yn 1829 a hwylio oedd y canolbwynt i ddechrau.
"Ond fe ddatblygodd e o fan'na i bob math o gystadlaethau fel rhwyfo ac yn 1886 roedd cystadleuaeth nofio a dala hwyaid. Mae pethau wedi datblygu tipyn bach ers hynny ond mae'r hwyl a sbri wedi parhau.
Dathliad
"Ac wrth gwrs hefyd mae hwn yn ddathliad o'n treftadaeth ni. Cafodd Cei Newydd ei adeiladu oherwydd y môr a'r cychod a'r harbwr. Ac felly mae'n gyfle i ddathlu hynny.
"Mae'n hyfryd i weld y cychod yn rasio o lefydd fel Abergwaun, Aberteifi, Aberystwyth, Abersoch - fyddan nhw gyd yn cyrraedd. A wedyn bydd tri diwrnod o rasio fan hyn yn y bae yng Nghei Newydd."
Yn ogystal â rasio, mae cystadleuthau i'r ymwelwyr gan gynnwys cystadleuaeth adeiladu cestyll tywod, helfa drysor, nofio, caiacio a phadlfyrddio.
Ar ddiwedd tridiau prysur, bydd y trefnwyr yn cychwyn paratoi ar gyfer regata 2027: "Mae tipyn o waith trefnu," eglurai Huw. "Ac erbyn diwedd wythnos hyn byddwn ni'n dechrau y gwaith o drefnu blwyddyn nesaf.
"Mae lot o bobl ynghlwm â fe. Ac hefyd mae'n rhaid diolch i'r holl fusnesau yng Nghei Newydd sydd yn cefnogi ac yn noddi'r digwyddiad hefyd.
"Mae'n bwysig iawn. Mae'n denu lot o bobl i Gei Newydd, pobl sy'n cystadlu a phobl sy'n dod i fwynhau'r awyrgylch a watsho beth sy'n mynd ymlaen. Felly, mae'n bwysig i ddenu pobl 'ma.
"Ac mae'n bwysig hefyd achos mae'n dod â phobl at ei gilydd - pobl leol, ymwelwyr a'r gymuned hwylio ar draws Bae Ceredigion."

title: ‘Proof by Underpants’ offers a cheeky way to test soil
content:
You don’t necessarily need advanced sensor technology or fancy tools to assess the health of the soil just beneath your feet. As ecologists and around 1,000 citizen scientists in Switzerland recently demonstrated, sometimes all that’s required is a pair of undies and a shovel.
In 2021, a team at the University of Zurich (UZH) partnered with the country’s federal agricultural research center, Agroscope, to launch Beweisstück Unterhose, aka Proof By Underpants. The mission was simple—gather as many volunteers as possible and direct them to bury a combination of cotton underwear and clean tea bags at roughly 1,000 strategically selected locations around Switzerland. Participants then retrieved the items two months later, photographed their decomposition progress, and mailed them to a lab along with a soil sample.
This wasn’t some type of meta-performance art project. Instead, researchers hoped to highlight the ecological importance of soil health, while also gaining a better sense of current ground conditions around the country. The findings and an underwear map, recently published in the journal Plants, People, Planet, showcase a range of soil health and a path towards better land management.
“Our results show that how soil is managed can significantly affect both soil life and soil quality,” UZH agroecologist Marcel van der Heijden said in a statement. “Healthy, biologically active soil is crucial for fertility, nutrient cycling and many other ecosystem services.”
Van der Heijden’s team reported that the fastest decomposing underwear was buried in residential gardens. These spots also had the highest levels of organic matter needed for vital bacteria, fungi, earthworms, and other underground organisms. Farmlands and meadows ranked slightly less organically active, while manicured lawns easily took last place.
This doesn’t mean that a region’s optimal underground environment is always one that facilitates rapid decomposition. Although desirable for agricultural land, other locations don’t necessarily benefit from so much organic activity in soil.
“In near-natural habitats such as forests, very high nutrient levels can indicate disruptions to the natural balance of nutrients,” added Agroscope agroecologist and study co-author Franz Bender.
This is also often the case for gardens, which can suffer from an overabundance of nutrients.
Researchers aren’t suggesting that the easiest method to assess your garden’s wellbeing is by burying a pair of underwear. But it remains a cheeky reminder that the benefits from healthy soil make themselves known quicker than you might expect.

title: OpenAI lance ChatGPT pour les adolescents, avec des outils de contrôle parental
content:
OpenAI annonce le déploiement progressif de ChatGPT pour les adolescents dans le monde entier, une version qui s’active automatiquement pour les moins de 18 ans et permet aux parents de régler des plages horaires d’utilisation, sans accès aux conversations.
ChatGPT pour les adolescents s’active automatiquement dès lors que les informations d’âge fournies sur le compte, la vérification d’âge ou la prédiction d’âge indiquent que l’utilisateur a moins de 18 ans.
Le service repose sur les mêmes fonctions d’IA que le ChatGPT classique, mais s’en distingue par l’ajout de fonctionnalités destinées à soutenir l’apprentissage, la création et la vie quotidienne des adolescents, ainsi que de dispositifs de protection adaptés à leur âge.
Le mode Étude et les Heures d’étude au cœur du dispositif
Les jeunes utilisateurs peuvent recourir au « mode Étude » pour obtenir des indices, des explications par étapes et des questions de relance. Le service propose aussi des quiz et d’autres outils permettant de s’entraîner sur les contenus étudiés et de vérifier sa compréhension. Lorsqu’un utilisateur pose une question liée à un devoir, ChatGPT peut l’orienter vers le mode Étude. Une fonction « Heures d’étude » est également introduite : lorsque l’adolescent ou le parent/tuteur associé au compte définit une plage horaire donnée, toute nouvelle conversation démarrée durant cette période débute automatiquement en mode Étude.
Des fonctions destinées à limiter les effets d’un usage prolongé sont également incluses. Des messages peuvent rappeler que ChatGPT est un outil d’IA ou inviter l’utilisateur à faire une pause. Avant l’envoi de certaines images, le service invite également à vérifier qu’elles ne contiennent pas d’informations personnelles ou sensibles.
Des heures calmes réglables par les parents, sans accès aux messages
Des fonctions de gestion optionnelles sont proposées aux parents et tuteurs. Une fois les comptes du parent et de l’adolescent associés, le tuteur peut gérer certains paramètres, notamment définir des « Heures calmes », limitant l’usage de ChatGPT pendant une période donnée. Les Heures d’étude peuvent elles aussi être définies non seulement par l’adolescent, mais aussi par le parent ou le tuteur associé. Les parents ne peuvent toutefois pas lire directement ni surveiller les conversations de leur enfant. OpenAI précise ne partager, dans les situations limitées où une alerte de sécurité est envoyée, que les informations strictement nécessaires pour soutenir la sécurité de l’adolescent.
Un retour au ChatGPT classique à la majorité
ChatGPT pour les adolescents applique par ailleurs, par défaut, des dispositifs de sécurité adaptés à l’âge, destinés à réduire l’exposition des adolescents à des contenus sensibles ou potentiellement dangereux. Lorsqu’un utilisateur est confirmé comme ayant 18 ans ou plus, son compte peut basculer vers l’environnement ChatGPT classique, ce qui peut entraîner la levée des protections propres aux adolescents ainsi que la fin des fonctions de gestion associées aux parents ou tuteurs.

title: Junior D’Tigress battle Mali in U-18 AfroBasket final
content:
Nigeria’s Junior D’Tigress will battle Mali in the final of the 2026 FIBA U18 Women’s AfroBasket on Sunday (today), having secured their place in the title match and a ticket to the 2027 FIBA U-19 Women’s Basketball World Cup in China with a 53-50 semi-final victory over hosts Ivory Coast on Friday, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.
The final, scheduled for the Palais des Sports dome in Treichville, will be a repeat of the 2024 championship match, in which Mali defeated Nigeria 76-56 in Pretoria, South Africa, to lift the title.
Against Ivory Coast, the Junior D’Tigress showed composure in a tight contest that went down to the wire.
Nigeria edged the first quarter 12-11 before extending their lead to 27-23 at halftime. They maintained control in the third quarter, winning it 14-13 to lead 41-36, before holding off a fierce late rally, in which the hosts won the fourth quarter 12-11, to close out a three-point win.
Favour Joy Anari led Nigeria’s scoring with 15 points, four assists and five steals, while Oluwatobiloba Owolabi added 11 points, including three of four attempts from beyond the arc. Nimah Ibidunni dominated the boards with 12 rebounds and six points, and Zainab Adelaja contributed six points, 10 rebounds and four assists.
Mali reached the final with a 57-55 semi-final win over Egypt and go into Sunday’s match as reigning champions chasing a tenth AfroBasket title in the age category. They have won nine titles and two silver medals in the competition’s history, compared with Nigeria’s two silver medals.
Mali topped their group unbeaten, defeating Benin 124-20, Morocco 103-30 and Egypt 62-57, before thrashing Kenya 93-22 in the quarter-final. Maimouna Traore, Suzane Dembele, Assan Mariko, Couda Keita and Aminata Samake have been Mali’s key players in Abidjan.
Nigeria, on the other hand, finished the group stage with a 2-1 record, having beaten Tunisia 54-50 and Senegal 70-40, and lost 75-74 to Cameroon. They avenged that defeat in the quarter-final, beating Cameroon 75-45, before edging Ivory Coast in the last-four. Coach Peter Akindele is expected to rely on Anari, Adelaja, Owolabi, Ibidunni, Bisola Arowolo and Khadijah Alli for the final.
Owolabi said the Junior D’Tigress were determined to change the narrative against Mali on Sunday.
“We’re aware that they are the defending champions and beat Nigeria in the 2024 final, but it will not be easy for Mali this time. As a team, we’re determined to change the narrative this time,” she said.
Both teams have already secured their places at the 2027 World Cup in China, meaning Sunday’s clash is solely for continental bragging rights.
Meanwhile, the National Sports Commission has congratulated the Junior D’Tigress for qualifying for the World Cup, describing their semi-final win over Ivory Coast as a demonstration of resilience in a difficult environment.
Director General of the NSC, Bukola Olopade, commended the board of the Nigeria Basketball Federation, led by President Musa Kida, for the progressive success recorded by the country’s national teams, particularly the women’s teams.
“The girls have done very well to secure their place at the Women’s World Cup in China next year, which shows their commitment, patriotism and discipline. Now that the World Cup ticket has been secured, I have no doubt that they can win the AfroBasket in Sunday’s final against Mali,” Olopade said.
The qualification of the Junior D’Tigress follows that of the senior team, D’Tigress, who also qualified for the FIBA Women’s World Cup in Germany, scheduled for September 2026.

title: How to better forecast once-in-a-millennium weather events
content:
For all that day-to-day weather forecasts have improved, it remains a challenge to forecast events that might happen once in 1,000 years—like the deadliest heat waves.
Traditional supercomputer-based models can forecast these events, but they require a lot of time and energy. Meanwhile, newer forecasting models, based on artificial intelligence, are good at day-to-day forecasts but often fail to predict outlier events that weren't represented in their training data.
"AI weather and climate models are one of the great achievements of AI in science, but they're not magical—they fail on gray swans, the rarest and most extreme events," said Pedram Hassanzadeh, University of Chicago associate professor of geophysical sciences. "Detailed physics-based models can capture extremes, but they require prohibitively large amounts of time and energy."
An international team of researchers in the United States and France, co-led by members of Hassanzadeh's Climate Extremes Theory and Data Group, has developed a new hybrid method, published in Physical Review Letters, to solve the problem.
Their solution marries the efficiency of AI tools with the trustworthiness of traditional models to help predict the odds of rare events quickly and accurately while using far fewer resources.
"The power of this method," Hassanzadeh said, "is that it combines the strengths of both AI and traditional physics and is particularly effective for extreme events, which are the hardest to simulate and have the greatest societal impact."
The statistics of rare events
Heat waves are one of the deadliest forms of extreme weather. In 2003, a heat wave led to roughly 70,000 deaths across Europe, and Russia suffered 56,000 deaths in 2010. This past June, nearly half of the United States—roughly 180 million people—experienced dangerous temperatures.
These waves are becoming increasingly frequent and severe, but the nature of outlier events makes them difficult to study and challenging to predict.
Forecasting has long relied on physics-based climate and weather models. They help us see how different conditions, like atmospheric pressure, might affect temperature and other variables over time. These models compute many different potential scenarios, which researchers use to see what is most likely to occur.
The trouble is that if you want to know the odds that Chicago will reach 90°F (32°C) in July—which is not uncommon—you wouldn't need to run many simulations before one landed on that temperature. But if you want to know the odds that it will reach 105°F (41°C), you'll need to try many more times before you see that extreme. Running that many simulations takes a lot of time and computational power.
Researchers can mitigate the issue by using a statistical technique called rare event sampling (RES), which speeds up the process by scoring conditions so the climate model can focus only on the most promising and ignore the rest. However, rare event sampling doesn't work well for short-duration events, like weeklong heat waves, rather than an entire season that is unusually hot overall.
To address this, the team came up with a new method named AI+RES, which boosts the scoring mechanism by adding AI's ability to predict which conditions are most likely to lead to shorter, rapidly developing extremes.
"After doing this iteratively, you eventually get to a bunch of simulations that do indeed capture whatever rare extreme event that you're interested in," said Alexander Wikner, Schmidt AI in Science Postdoctoral Fellow in Hassanzadeh's group and co-first author on the study. "The more you get, the better you can estimate the probability of that event, and that ultimately gives you a lot more certainty."
To test the method, the team ran 50,000 simulations using a traditional climate model to predict heat waves over areas of France and the U.S. Midwest. Their new AI+RES method gave nearly identical results using one-hundredth as many simulations.
Because this work was a proof of concept, they used a model that didn't take into account climate change, which adds another level of complexity. The researchers hope to test their method on models running under different climate change scenarios to see how results might shift as the planet warms.
Wikner notes that the method could also help generate rare-event data sets to train even better AI models, which would then speed up their method even further.
Scaling up
According to the scientists, the hybrid method could be applied to other severe weather, including tropical cyclones or extreme precipitation.
"What I like about this framework," Hassanzadeh said, "is that it's ready to be scaled. AI models trained on real weather observations are already built and in use, so the next step is to connect a state-of-the-art numerical weather or climate prediction model to one of them through this algorithm."
This would give decision-makers access to accurate information they need, like the frequency of strong storms and heat waves in the current and future climate at regional scales—such as over Texas, Florida or California.
"This is exactly the kind of information federal, state and local governments need as a first step for climate adaptation and mitigation planning," added Hassanzadeh. "It's very exciting that we could be scaling this up into real-world models that directly provide such information to the public and to policymakers."

title: Tập đoàn Vinacam trao 3,5 tỉ đồng Tiếp sức đến trường: Nghĩ đến có SV bỏ học là công ty cố gắng
content:
Nguồn kinh phí này tương đương với 180 suất học bổng Tiếp sức đến trường cùng 50 laptop được trích từ Quỹ khuyến học Vinacam “Nâng bước tri thức Việt” do công ty cùng các đối tác, đại lý, nhà hảo tâm đóng góp.
“Nghĩ đến việc có thêm một bạn không thể đến trường, chúng tôi luôn cố gắng nhiều hơn"
Ông Vũ Hải Sơn - Phó tổng giám đốc Công ty cổ phần Tập đoàn Vinacam - cho biết năm 2026 đánh dấu 20 năm Vinacam và Quỹ Khuyến học Vinacam đồng hành cùng báo Tuổi Trẻ trong chương trình Tiếp sức đến trường. Sau 20 năm, tổng số tiền đóng góp cho chương trình của công ty đã hơn 1 triệu USD.
Công ty cổ phần Tập đoàn Vinacam trao 3,5 tỉ đồng cho học bổng Tiếp sức đến trường - Video: TRƯƠNG KIÊN - XUÂN TIÊN
“Các bạn tân sinh viên khó khăn hãy tiếp tục cố gắng học tập. Hãy xem sự đóng góp của chúng tôi và xã hội như một niềm tin dành cho các bạn. Chỉ cần các bạn nỗ lực vươn lên, xã hội sẽ tạo điều kiện để các bạn thực hiện ước mơ của mình”, ông Sơn nói.
Chương trình Tiếp sức đến trường là một chương trình có ý nghĩa sâu sắc, được duy trì và tổ chức bền bỉ trong nhiều năm, qua đó chứng minh hiệu quả và sức ảnh hưởng xã hội đối với học sinh, sinh viên có hoàn cảnh khó khăn trên cả nước.
Năm nay, trong bối cảnh chi phí xăng dầu, hàng hóa và các nhu yếu phẩm đều tăng, nhiều doanh nghiệp trong và ngoài nước cũng gặp khó khăn, nguồn đóng góp từ các nhà hảo tâm, tài trợ giảm so với những năm trước. Tuy nhiên, Vinacam và Quỹ Khuyến học Vinacam vẫn cố gắng gồng gánh để tăng mức đóng góp cho các bạn sinh viên.
“Các tân sinh viên năm nào cũng cần cố gắng để được đi học. Nếu chúng tôi không cố gắng, mà dừng lại, biết đâu sẽ có thêm một bạn học sinh không thể đến trường. Nghĩ đến điều đó khiến chúng tôi phải cố gắng dành dụm, làm việc nhiều hơn để có thể đóng góp cho các bạn nhiều hơn”, ông Sơn nói.
Những năm tiếp theo, ông Sơn khẳng định công ty sẽ duy trì đồng hành với chương trình Tiếp sức đến trường của báo Tuổi Trẻ.
Đến với các SV nghèo là Vinacam thực sự sẻ chia
Ông Trịnh Thanh Dũng - Giám đốc kinh doanh Công ty cổ phần Tập đoàn Vinacam - cho biết bên cạnh việc duy trì, tăng mức đóng góp hằng năm, công ty mong muốn kết nối thêm các doanh nghiệp, đơn vị cùng tâm huyết để trực tiếp đồng hành với báo Tuổi Trẻ, qua đó huy động thêm nguồn lực hỗ trợ tân sinh viên khó khăn.
Ông Dũng mong muốn sự đồng hành cùng Tiếp sức đến trường ngày càng được lan tỏa đến thế hệ trẻ.
Các bạn trẻ hôm nay, đặc biệt những người thường xuyên tiếp cận thông tin trên báo điện tử, sẽ là thế hệ tiếp nối những giá trị tốt đẹp và tinh thần sẻ chia mà chương trình đã xây dựng.
“Mục tiêu quan trọng nhất không chỉ giúp các em đến trường mà còn giáo dục để sau này các em trưởng thành, sống tử tế, sống tốt và nhớ rằng đã từng có những người đồng hành, giúp đỡ mình trong một giai đoạn khó khăn của cuộc đời”, ông Dũng bày tỏ.
Sự gắn bó chân tình và bền bỉ
Nhà báo Nguyễn Hoàng Nguyên - Phó tổng biên tập báo Tuổi Trẻ - trân trọng sự đồng hành bền bỉ của Tập đoàn Vinacam với chương trình Tiếp sức đến trường suốt 20 năm qua, đặc biệt trong bối cảnh nhiều doanh nghiệp đang gặp khó khăn.
Nhà báo Nguyễn Hoàng Nguyên bày tỏ sự chung tay của Vinacam không chỉ góp thêm nguồn lực để hỗ trợ tân sinh viên khó khăn mà còn lan tỏa tinh thần sẻ chia, trách nhiệm với cộng đồng.
“Vinacam là một trong những đơn vị luôn gắn bó chân tình với chương trình và các bạn sinh viên khó khăn.
Chúng tôi rất trân trọng sự đồng hành này và kỳ vọng chương trình Tiếp sức đến trường năm nay sẽ tạo dấu ấn xã hội tốt hơn nữa, để Vinacam và các nhà hảo tâm cảm nhận rõ ý nghĩa của những đóng góp thiết thực dành cho các bạn tân sinh viên”, nhà báo Nguyễn Hoàng Nguyên nói.
Ông cho biết chương trình Tiếp sức đến trường 2026 được triển khai trong mô hình mới của báo Tuổi Trẻ, tăng cường truyền thông trên nền tảng số. Qua đó, chương trình không chỉ vận động học bổng mà còn lan tỏa tinh thần sẻ chia, giúp gen Z hiểu hơn về những bạn trẻ đồng trang lứa đang khó khăn trên hành trình đến trường của các tân sinh viên nghèo hiếu học.
Báo Tuổi Trẻ trân trọng mời bạn đọc tài trợ cho học bổng Tiếp sức đến trường:
Học bổng bằng tiền mặt hoặc hỗ trợ miễn, giảm học phí cho tân sinh viên.
Thiết bị học tập như: máy tính xách tay, ba lô, sách vở, dụng cụ học tập, gói dữ liệu Internet và các phương tiện phục vụ học tập.
Phương tiện đi lại như xe đạp, xe gắn máy hoặc các hình thức hỗ trợ phù hợp khác.
Các khóa học ngoại ngữ, kỹ năng mềm, kỹ năng nghề nghiệp, chương trình đào tạo và phát triển năng lực cho tân sinh viên.
Kết nối cơ hội thực tập, việc làm bán thời gian, chỗ ở miễn phí hoặc các chính sách hỗ trợ khác.
Đồng hành trên nền tảng số thông qua việc quyên góp trực tuyến thông qua mã QR, tài khoản ngân hàng hoặc nền tảng thanh toán số.
Mời các cựu sinh viên từng nhận học bổng "Tiếp sức đến trường" trở lại đồng hành bằng nhiều hình thức như hỗ trợ học bổng, chia sẻ kinh nghiệm hoặc giới thiệu cơ hội thực tập, việc làm cho tân sinh viên…
